section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
section_1.content: Briefly define 'Distribution' as a shape showing how data spreads. Introduce the 'Uniform' (flat) and 'Skewed' (lopsided) distributions to establish that data doesn't always look like a bell curve.
section_1.example: Visualizing a die roll: Rolling one die gives a flat distribution (equal chance for 1-6).

section_2.title: The Problem: Chaos in Small Samples
section_2.content: Explain that when we look at individual data points, they are unpredictable and follow the original, irregular distribution. This is the 'Chaos' phase.
section_2.example: An anthropomorphic squirrel collecting nuts: One day he might find 0 nuts, the next he finds 20. His personal success is highly erratic.

section_3.title: The Mechanism: The Power of Aggregation
section_3.content: Introduce the CLT: As we increase the sample size (n) and take the average of those samples, the distribution of those averages begins to morph into a 'Normal Distribution' (Bell Curve), regardless of the original data shape.
section_3.example: The 'Squirrel Council': Instead of tracking one squirrel, we track the average of 50 squirrels. The extreme '0 nuts' and '20 nuts' days cancel each other out, forming a predictable peak at the average.

section_4.title: Visualization: The Morphing Animation
section_4.content: Describe a visual transition: Start with a jagged, irregular histogram. As a counter 'n' increases from 1 to 30, show the bars shifting and smoothing out into a perfect symmetrical Bell Curve.
section_4.example: An animation showing a 'chaos cloud' of dots collapsing into a neat, symmetrical mountain shape as more samples are added.

section_5.title: Application: Why Does This Matter?
section_5.content: Conclude with the real-world significance: The CLT allows us to make predictions about populations based on samples, forming the backbone of inferential statistics and quality control.
section_5.example: Factory QC: A sensor measures the weight of thousands of candy bars. Even if the machine is slightly inconsistent, the average weight will perfectly follow a bell curve, telling the factory exactly how many bars to reject.

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=32, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        formatted_lines = [f"- {line}" for line in lecture_lines]
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=24, color=WHITE) for line in formatted_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.4).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.4)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 2.0 + j * 1.2
                y = 2.2 - i * 0.9
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.setup_layout("The Mechanism: The Power of Aggregation", [
            "Aggregation reveals the hidden structure.",
            "Averages smooth out extreme values.",
            "Many averages form a Bell Curve."
        ])
        
        # Objects
        circles = VGroup(*[Circle(radius=0.3, fill_opacity=0.6) for _ in range(3)])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(circles.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.5)))
        self.place_at_grid(circles, 'B2')
        self.play(circles.animate.set_color("#1ABC9C"))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#1ABC9C")
        self.wait(1)

        self.play(FadeIn(avg_indicator))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#2980B9")
        self.wait(1)

        self.place_in_area(bell, 'C4', 'E6')
        self.play(Create(bell))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#F39C12")
        self.wait(2)
